newsitem.title: USA: Centennial Tech ex-CEO remains in custody.
newsitem.headline: Centennial Tech ex-CEO remains in custody.

text.p: The former chief executive of last year's best-performing company on the New York Stock Exchange -- Centennial Technologies Inc -- remained in federal custody on Tuesday after a detention hearing.

U.S. Magistrate Lawrence Cohen heard that Centennial would restate its earnings for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1996, as well as the first two quarters of fiscal year 1997, to show losses of more than $10 million. That is more than the amount the computer card maker first reported in profit.
As the litany of the company's fiscal failures continued, Centennial's former chief executive, Emanuel Pinez, 59, sat in the first row of spectators shaking his head of gray hair.

Looking tired beneath a tan, Pinez, an Israeli citizen with a wife in Switzerland, a home in Montreal, two houses and another family in Massachusetts, learned he would face at least three years in prison if convicted of charges filed against him, which include insider trading, overstating revenue and manipulating inventory.

FBI agent Robert Turgiss testified at the detention hearing that Pinez owed Lehman Brothers and PaineWebber Group Inc more than $20 million borrowed "on margin" based on the market value of the stock in his accounts. The stock was primarily shares in Centennial.

His lawyer, Robert Ullmann, attempted to argue that put and call options for Centennial stock, which Pinez began buying three days before he was dismissed on February 10, were acquired not at his client's request, but because of pressure from the two firms.

But Judge Cohen cut Ullmann off. "This is not La-La land. This is not O.J.," Cohen said, referring to the O.J. Simpson case. "I will assume unless there is evidence to the contrary that the puts and calls were done by Mr. Pinez."

The Securities and Exchange Commission, in a separate case, has charged that Pinez stood to gain $447,500 from the 2,400 "call" option contracts he bought on Centennial stock. The SEC said the value of the 1,955 "put" options, which expire March 21, could not yet be determined.
"If the value of Centennial stock went down, Mr. Pinez would gain, is that correct?" Judge Cohen asked Turgiss, who replied, "The further Centennial declines, the more Mr. Pinez earns."
But it is unclear if Pinez, or any other Centennial investor, will have a chance to earn any money from the stock.

On Tuesday, the New York Stock Exchange, which halted trading in the shares on February 11, said it would suspend trading of the common stock on March 3 and apply to federal regulators to delist the stock.

Centennial shares resumed trading on Tuesday. The issue opened at 4-1/8, off about 75 percent from their last trade eight days ago, when they closed at 16-3/8. It finished the session at 2-7/8, down 13-1/2. In 1996, the shares rose 451 percent to 52.
The magistrate did not rule on bail and until he does, Pinez will remain in custody.
